_note: Soil-test rating classes and recommended fertiliser doses. Ratings are the standard ICAR / Soil Health Card classes used by state soil-testing laboratories in India. Doses are general recommendations for Maharashtra at the district level and are NOT a substitute for a soil health card or a local KVK recommendation — PRAHARI says so on every response. An agronomist can open a pull request against this file without touching any Python.

sources.ratings: Soil Health Card scheme rating classes, Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India; ICAR soil-test rating conventions (available N by alkaline permanganate, P by Olsen, K by ammonium acetate).
sources.doses: General recommended doses of fertiliser (RDF) for Maharashtra, as published in state agricultural university package-of-practice literature. Indicative only.
sources.adjustment: Soil-test-crop-response practice: a LOW rating raises the dose by about a quarter, a HIGH rating lowers it by about a quarter, relative to the general recommendation.
sources.units: Doses are stated per ACRE. State package-of-practice literature publishes them per hectare; these are the hectare figures divided by 2.47. If you are comparing with a printed recommendation, check which unit it uses — the difference is a factor of two and a half, and it is the most common arithmetic error on a fertiliser bill.

organic_carbon_pct.means_low: Low organic matter. This is the single biggest lever on this list — it holds water, feeds soil life and releases nitrogen slowly all season.
organic_carbon_pct.means_high: Good organic matter. Keep doing whatever you are doing.

nitrogen_kg_ha.means_low: Low available nitrogen — normal for most Maharashtra soils and the reason nitrogen is applied every season.
nitrogen_kg_ha.means_high: High available nitrogen. Cutting the nitrogen dose saves money AND reduces sucking-pest pressure, because soft nitrogen-rich growth is what whitefly and aphids prefer.

phosphorus_kg_ha.means_low: Low phosphorus. Roots and early establishment suffer first, and the symptom looks like poor vigour rather than anything specific.
phosphorus_kg_ha.means_high: High phosphorus. Applying more locks up zinc and iron; a full-dose DAP habit on a high-P soil is money spent to create a micronutrient problem.

potassium_kg_ha.means_low: Low potassium. Potassium is what thickens cell walls, so a deficient crop is measurably more susceptible to disease and to water stress.

ph.means_low: Acidic. Phosphorus availability drops and aluminium can become toxic below 5.5.
ph.means_high: Alkaline to sodic. Iron and zinc lock up; gypsum and organic matter are the usual correction, and a sodic soil needs a proper laboratory recommendation, not an app.

tomato.split: Half the nitrogen and all the phosphorus and potassium at transplanting; the rest of the nitrogen in two splits at flowering and first fruit set.

onion.split: Half the nitrogen basal with all the phosphorus and potassium; the rest 30 and 45 days after transplanting. Stop nitrogen once bulbing starts or the bulbs will not store.

grape.split: Split across the season after pruning; potassium matters most through berry development.

maize.split: One third of the nitrogen basal, one third at knee height, one third before tasselling.

cotton.split: One third basal, the rest at squaring and at boll development.

soybean.split: All basal. Soybean fixes most of its own nitrogen — a heavy nitrogen dose suppresses nodulation and wastes the money twice.

pigeonpea.split: All basal. Like soybean, this is a legume; the nitrogen is a starter dose, not a feeding programme.

straights.name: Single super phosphate (SSP)
straights.note: 16% P2O5, and it also carries sulphur and calcium

options.label: It breaks into a few large clods
It stays as one hard block
